events.title: SQL database language invented
events.summary: In May 1974, Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce published SEQUEL — the query language that became SQL for asking questions of relational databases.
events.about: SQL (originally spelled SEQUEL) is how apps read and update structured data — `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `JOIN`, and `GROUP BY`. Every web app, bank, and analytics pipeline ultimately talks SQL or a close variant (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server).

narrative.whyChosen: This paper turned the relational database idea into a practical language anyone could learn to fetch and combine data.
narrative.whyImportant: SQL became the universal way to talk to databases — still the dominant interface to structured data fifty years later.
narrative.problemSolved: Old database APIs forced programmers to describe step-by-step paths through records; SEQUEL let them simply say what data they wanted.

sources.title: ACM — SEQUEL: A Structured English Query Language (May 1, 1974)

events.title: Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn publish TCP/IP design
events.summary: Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn published A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication in May 1974 — defining the TCP design that became the internet's foundation.
events.about: The paper described how heterogeneous packet networks could interconnect with reliable end-to-end communication — later split into TCP and IP. Every HTTP request still rides protocols descended from this work.

narrative.whyChosen: The Cerf–Kahn paper is the architectural birth certificate of the internet protocol suite.
narrative.whyImportant: It enabled internetworking beyond any single vendor or network technology.
narrative.problemSolved: Packet networks could not share resources or route across incompatible systems.

sources.title: IEEE — A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication (May 1974)
